nodes.title: Operations objectives and performance trade-offs

teaching_content.core_explanation: Operations is the part of a business system that designs, runs and improves the processes that turn inputs into goods and services. Operational performance is commonly judged through cost, quality, speed, dependability and flexibility, but those dimensions are not independent. More spare capacity can improve speed and resilience while increasing unit cost. Extreme standardisation can reduce variation and cost but weaken customisation. Very low inventory can release cash while increasing the risk of stockouts or production disruption. Strong operations decisions therefore begin with the customer value proposition and business strategy: a low-cost airline, emergency hospital, bespoke architect and luxury hotel require different operational priorities. The aim is not to maximise every performance dimension simultaneously, but to create a coherent operating system that delivers the outcomes the target customer values while remaining financially sustainable and resilient.
teaching_content.why_it_matters: This node gives learners the operating-performance lens needed to evaluate capacity, process, quality, inventory and supply-chain decisions rather than assuming lowest cost is always best.
definitions: operations: activities and processes that transform inputs into goods/services
cost objective: delivering required output with economical use of resources
quality: ability to meet relevant requirements and expectations
speed: time taken to deliver or respond
dependability: consistency/reliability of delivery
flexibility: ability to vary volume, mix, specification or timing
important_boundaries: low cost is not automatically operational excellence
quality does not simply mean luxury
high utilisation is not identical to efficiency
flexibility can create cost and complexity
facts: performance objectives often trade off in the short run
operational priorities should reflect customer needs and strategy
process design can create both direct cost and indirect service effects
mechanisms: additional capacity -> shorter queues/faster response but higher fixed-resource cost
standardisation -> lower variation/training complexity but lower customisation
greater flexibility -> broader response capability but more skills/process complexity
causal_relationships: customer promise -> operating requirements -> process/capacity/quality choices -> experience -> demand/financial outcome
local cost reduction -> possible quality/speed/resilience effect -> wider business consequence
examples: A same-day delivery service may accept lower average vehicle utilisation to preserve responsiveness; maximising utilisation could make its core promise impossible.
non_examples: Describing a warehouse as efficient solely because it runs at 100% capacity.
Assuming premium quality always requires expensive materials rather than reliable conformance to customer requirements.
applications: identify relevant operational objectives for a case
real_world_transfer: Explain why spare capacity can be economically rational.
Identify when a cost-saving measure undermines the customer's reason for buying.
assumptions: Performance dimensions need clear definitions and comparable measurement.
limitations: Performance objectives are simplifications; safety, sustainability and resilience may need explicit treatment alongside them.

misconceptions.correction: Operations should deliver the required mix of performance objectives for the strategy; the cheapest system can destroy customer value or resilience.

evidence_of_understanding: judge whether an operating system supports strategy

nodes.title: Production and process methods

teaching_content.core_explanation: Process choice determines how work is organised to produce goods or services. Job or project processes create highly customised outputs in low volumes, often using flexible skilled resources. Batch processes produce groups of similar items before changing to another product or task. Flow processes arrange work in a repeated sequence for high-volume, standardised output, while continuous processes are an extreme form designed to operate with very high continuity. Service processes can contain equivalent patterns even when no physical product moves along a line. Real businesses often combine process types. Automation is a technology choice rather than a process category: a robot can automate a repetitive task inside batch or flow production, while a highly customised job process may use sophisticated digital tools. Appropriate process choice depends on volume, variety, demand stability, required flexibility, skills, capital, quality and desired speed.
teaching_content.why_it_matters: Process design shapes cost, capacity, flexibility, quality, skills and investment requirements throughout the business.
definitions: job/project production: one-off or highly customised production
batch production: groups of similar outputs produced together
flow production: repeated sequential production at relatively high volume
continuous process: near-uninterrupted high-volume process
automation: use of technology to perform tasks with reduced direct human intervention
important_boundaries: automation is not synonymous with flow production
service operations also have process choices
no process method is universally best
high volume does not always require complete standardisation
facts: higher standardisation can support automation and lower unit cost
higher variety often requires flexibility and skills
changeovers in batch production create time/cost
mechanisms: volume/variety -> process design -> skills/capital/cost/flexibility
automation -> consistency/productivity potential -> capital/maintenance/skills implications
process mismatch -> queues, waste, poor quality or excess cost
causal_relationships: demand characteristics -> process choice -> cost/capacity/quality outcome
automation investment -> labour-task redesign -> productivity/skill/cash consequences
examples: A bespoke construction project uses job/project logic; a bakery may batch different products; a bottling line uses flow; a chemical plant can use continuous processing.
non_examples: Assuming batch is always inefficient because it involves changeovers.
applications: select a process for volume/variety context
real_world_transfer: Explain why a low-variety high-volume process can justify specialist capital equipment.
Identify why automating a poorly designed process can simply automate waste.
assumptions: Volume, variety and demand patterns are sufficiently understood for process design.
limitations: Modern flexible manufacturing and digital services blur traditional categories.

misconceptions.correction: Automation is a technology decision that can appear within different process types.

models_frameworks: volume-variety process continuum as a teaching representation

teaching_content.core_explanation: Capacity is the maximum sustainable output a process or system can produce over a stated period under defined conditions. Actual system capacity is often constrained by a bottleneck: the resource or stage with insufficient capacity relative to demand on it. Capacity utilisation compares actual output with available capacity. Higher utilisation can spread fixed costs and indicate strong demand, but very high utilisation can create queues, overtime, maintenance deferral, quality problems and reduced ability to absorb demand variability. Spare capacity therefore has an opportunity cost but can also create option value: it allows rapid response, maintenance, recovery from disruption and growth. Capacity decisions are often lumpy and long-term, so businesses can use overtime, subcontracting, flexible labour, appointment systems, yield management or demand shaping before committing to major fixed expansion.
teaching_content.why_it_matters: Capacity connects demand, cost, service, investment and resilience. It is a prime example of why one apparently favourable metric can become harmful when maximised mechanically.
definitions: capacity: maximum sustainable output under specified conditions
bottleneck: stage/resource limiting system throughput
capacity utilisation: actual output divided by capacity
spare capacity: unused capacity available in the period
important_boundaries: 100% utilisation is not automatically optimal
system capacity is determined by constraints rather than the sum of individual capacities
nominal/design capacity can exceed sustainable effective capacity
facts: variability causes queueing pressure at high utilisation
bottleneck improvement can increase system throughput more than improving non-bottlenecks
capacity expansion creates fixed cost and may take time
mechanisms: higher utilisation -> fixed cost spread but lower buffer -> queue/overtime/failure risk
bottleneck -> work accumulation -> delay -> customer/service effect
capacity investment -> higher fixed cost/cash requirement -> potential future growth/support
causal_relationships: demand increase -> utilisation -> queue/overtime -> quality/delivery -> customer response
capacity expansion -> cash/fixed cost -> lower utilisation initially -> higher response/growth capability
examples: A call centre with 98% staff utilisation may look productive but customers can face long waits because even small demand spikes have no buffer.
non_examples: Calling unused capacity waste without considering service/resilience objectives.
Adding capacity to a non-bottleneck machine and assuming total output will rise.
applications: trace utilisation into service and cost
real_world_transfer: Explain why 85% utilisation might outperform 100% for a time-sensitive service.
Identify which process stage should receive investment first.
assumptions: Capacity and actual output are measured on a consistent basis and product mix is comparable.
limitations: A single utilisation percentage can hide product mix, downtime, quality losses and shift constraints.

misconceptions.incorrect_belief: Higher capacity utilisation is always better.
misconceptions.correction: Very high utilisation can reduce speed, dependability, maintenance and resilience; the desirable level depends on the operating context.

methods.name: Capacity utilisation
methods.interpretation: The process used 85% of stated capacity during the period; whether that is desirable depends on demand variability, cost and service requirements.

worked_examples: A process has capacity 10,000 units and outputs 8,500: utilisation 85%, leaving 1,500 units apparent spare capacity before other constraints.
interpretation: Use alongside queues, quality, downtime and demand forecasts.
common_errors: assuming capacity is fixed regardless of product mix

teaching_content.core_explanation: Productivity relates output to the quantity of an input used, such as labour hours. Production is the absolute quantity produced. Efficiency is broader: it concerns how economically resources are converted into the required outcomes, including waste, quality and cost. A business can increase production while productivity falls if inputs rise faster than output. It can raise measured productivity by speeding work while damaging quality, so comparable output quality matters. Labour productivity is often measured as output per worker or per labour hour; output per hour is generally more informative where hours vary. Unit economics connects operational output to financial performance by examining revenue, contribution or cost at the unit/customer/order level. Productivity improvements can come from training, process redesign, technology, better management, product simplification or removing bottlenecks, but their effect depends on whether demand exists for the additional output and whether quality is maintained.
teaching_content.why_it_matters: Productivity is central to competitiveness and living/business performance, but it is commonly confused with production or treated as an automatically positive number.
definitions: production: total amount of output produced
productivity: output per unit of input
labour productivity: output per worker or labour hour
efficiency: resource performance relative to required outcomes
unit economics: revenue/cost/contribution relationships at a defined unit of activity
important_boundaries: production is not productivity
productivity is not identical to efficiency
higher measured productivity can hide quality decline
unit cost can fall while total cost rises
facts: productivity measures require consistent output/input definitions
automation can raise productivity while changing skill/capital needs
quality losses and rework reduce effective productivity
mechanisms: training/process/technology -> more good output per input -> potential unit-cost improvement
higher output without demand -> inventory/cash problem
speed pressure -> defects/rework -> apparent versus real productivity divergence
causal_relationships: productivity initiative -> workload/quality/motivation -> sustainable or temporary performance
examples: 9,000 good units produced in 300 labour hours gives 30 good units per labour hour. If 10,000 units are produced but 1,500 require rework, headline output alone overstates useful productivity.
non_examples: Saying production rose from 1,000 to 1,200 units so productivity increased without knowing labour/input use.
applications: evaluate productivity initiatives with quality and demand
real_world_transfer: Challenge a productivity claim based only on gross output when defect/rework rates changed.
Explain why higher productivity can release capacity but not guarantee higher profit.
assumptions: Output units are comparable and quality differences are accounted for sufficiently.
limitations: Multi-factor productivity is more complex; service output can be difficult to quantify; short-run measures may encourage dysfunctional work intensity.

misconceptions.correction: Productivity depends on output relative to input; both can rise while productivity falls.

methods.name: Labour productivity
methods.units: units per worker or labour hour
methods.worked_example: 9,000 good units / 300 labour hours = 30 units per labour hour
methods.interpretation: Each labour hour produced 30 good units under the stated measurement basis.

worked_examples: If output rises 10% but labour hours rise 15%, labour productivity falls despite higher production.
interpretation: Compare like-for-like output quality and input definition.
common_errors: mixing workers and labour hours inconsistently

nodes.title: Lean operations, waste and continuous improvement

teaching_content.core_explanation: Lean operations is a family of ideas focused on improving the flow of customer value while reducing avoidable waste. Waste can appear as defects, waiting, unnecessary movement, excess processing, overproduction, excess inventory or underused capability. Continuous improvement means repeatedly identifying problems, investigating causes, testing changes, measuring effects and standardising successful improvements rather than relying only on occasional major projects. Lean should not be reduced to cutting staff or eliminating every buffer. Some apparent 'non-value-adding' activities—maintenance, safety checks, training, contingency capacity—protect the system and can be economically necessary. Just-in-time approaches aim to reduce inventory and expose process problems by receiving/producing closer to actual need, but they increase dependence on reliable processes, suppliers and information. Lean therefore works best as system improvement, not as local cost cutting.
teaching_content.why_it_matters: Lean demonstrates how process, quality, inventory, culture and problem-solving interact, and why removing visible cost without understanding system effects can make performance worse.
definitions: lean operations: systematic pursuit of customer value with reduced avoidable waste
waste: resource use that does not add required value or protect necessary system capability
continuous improvement: repeated incremental problem-solving and learning
just in time: approach that reduces inventory/production timing buffers by responding closely to actual need
important_boundaries: lean is not simply job cutting
zero inventory is not automatically optimal
maintenance/safety can be necessary even when not directly billable
continuous improvement requires measurement and learning, not constant change for its own sake
facts: waste often crosses functional boundaries
lower buffers expose process variability
employee knowledge can be important for identifying root causes
mechanisms: waste removal -> shorter flow/lower cost -> capacity improvement
lower inventory -> cash release but greater reliability dependence
employee problem-solving -> local knowledge -> process improvement
causal_relationships: lean change -> lower buffer -> problems become visible -> improvement opportunity or disruption if reliability weak
examples: A manufacturer reduces batch sizes only after improving changeover reliability; otherwise more frequent setups would create downtime rather than lean flow.
non_examples: Cutting maintenance because it is 'non-value adding' and then experiencing more breakdowns.
applications: distinguish local cost cutting from system improvement
real_world_transfer: Recognise when a claimed lean programme is merely headcount reduction.
Explain why lower inventory can improve cash and simultaneously raise supply risk.
assumptions: Demand/process information is reliable enough and suppliers/processes can support reduced buffers.
limitations: Extreme leanness can reduce resilience; some sectors require safety stocks and redundancy.

misconceptions.incorrect_belief: Lean means removing all spare capacity and inventory.
misconceptions.correction: Lean removes avoidable waste while preserving capabilities needed for customer value, safety and resilience.

interpretation: lean outcomes should be measured across quality, flow, cost and inventory rather than one local metric

models_frameworks: waste categories / continuous-improvement cycle as teaching aids

nodes.title: Inventory and service trade-offs

teaching_content.core_explanation: Inventory is stock held for future use or sale, including raw materials, work in progress and finished goods. Inventory can protect production and customer service by buffering uncertainty in demand, supply or processing. It also ties up cash and creates storage, insurance, damage, shrinkage and obsolescence risks. Inventory decisions therefore balance service and resilience against working-capital and carrying costs. Buffer stock protects against variability; reorder decisions determine when replenishment should be triggered; lead time affects how early orders must be placed. Just-in-time approaches seek to reduce inventory by improving synchronisation and reliability, but they do not make uncertainty disappear. Inventory also illustrates the difference between accounting assets and liquidity: stock may be recorded as a current asset but cannot necessarily be converted quickly into cash at its recorded value.
teaching_content.why_it_matters: Inventory links operations to cash flow, customer service, supply-chain risk and profitability.
definitions: inventory: goods/materials held for production or sale
raw materials: inputs not yet processed
work in progress: partially completed output
finished goods: completed output awaiting sale/delivery
buffer/safety stock: inventory held to absorb uncertainty
lead time: time between initiating replenishment and receiving/using it
important_boundaries: inventory is not cash
low inventory is not automatically efficient
high inventory can indicate poor forecasting or deliberate resilience
JIT is an operating approach rather than a guarantee of zero stock
facts: inventory consumes working capital
longer/less reliable lead times generally increase the value of buffers
perishable/technology products face high obsolescence risk
mechanisms: more inventory -> higher availability/resilience but cash/storage cost
less inventory -> cash release but higher stockout/disruption risk
forecast error/lead-time variation -> buffer requirement
causal_relationships: demand uncertainty + lead time -> inventory policy -> stockout/service/cash outcomes
excess inventory -> working capital -> financing/cash pressure
examples: A seasonal retailer builds inventory before peak demand, accepting cash tied up in stock to avoid lost sales. A fashion retailer faces additional markdown risk if the forecast is wrong.
non_examples: Calling every unit of unsold stock a waste regardless of service and lead-time requirements.
real_world_transfer: Explain why a company can appear asset-rich and still be cash-poor because much of its current asset base is slow-moving stock.
assumptions: Demand, lead time and service targets can be estimated with useful reliability.
limitations: Simple stock-control diagrams can hide multi-product, capacity and supplier constraints.

misconceptions.incorrect_belief: Inventory is basically cash because it is a current asset.
misconceptions.correction: Inventory must be sold/used before becoming cash and may require discounting or become obsolete.

methods: basic inventory level/reorder calculations may be course-specific
interpretation: inventory measures require product and lead-time context
common_errors: treating lower stock as automatically better

models_frameworks: stock-control diagram where required by exact course
evidence_of_understanding: link lead time to inventory policy
uncertainties: Exact inventory-control calculation conventions vary by qualification.

nodes.title: Procurement, supply chains, logistics, transparency and traceability

teaching_content.core_explanation: Procurement is the process of obtaining external goods and services needed by the business. Supply-chain management coordinates the network of organisations, information, physical flows and financial flows involved in creating and delivering an offering. Logistics focuses particularly on transport, storage and movement. Supplier choice should be based on total value and risk rather than unit price alone. Quality, reliability, lead time, payment terms, minimum order quantities, transport, inventory needs, switching costs, ethical/environmental exposure and supplier financial resilience can all change the real cost. Supply-chain transparency is the ability to understand relevant actors, practices and conditions in the network; traceability is the ability to follow products/materials or information through that network. Transparency and traceability can support quality, compliance, sustainability claims and risk management, but collecting data does not automatically make a chain ethical or resilient. Businesses can use supplier codes, audits, certification, contractual requirements and closer supplier relationships, but each control has limits and cost.
teaching_content.why_it_matters: Supply chains link operations to cash, resilience, ethics, sustainability, globalisation and customer promises. Cheap purchasing can be economically expensive once system effects are included.
definitions: procurement: acquisition of external goods/services
supply chain: network of parties and flows involved in creating/delivering an offering
logistics: movement/storage of goods and related information
transparency: visibility of relevant supply-chain actors/practices
traceability: ability to follow materials/products/information through stages
responsible sourcing: procurement approach considering social/environmental/governance as well as commercial factors
important_boundaries: lowest purchase price is not lowest total cost
outsourcing supply does not outsource reputation
visibility is not the same as control
audit evidence is not proof that no problem exists
facts: payment terms affect both buyer and supplier working capital
long global chains can increase lead-time and disruption exposure
single sourcing can improve relationships/economies but increase dependency
mechanisms: supplier quality/reliability -> production/service performance -> customer outcome
long lead time -> inventory requirement -> cash exposure
traceability -> faster identification of source/problem -> recall/compliance/risk response
payment-term pressure -> supplier liquidity -> reliability/failure risk
causal_relationships: transparency -> better evidence -> improved control only if action follows
examples: A supplier offering 5% lower unit price but requiring large minimum orders and 12-week lead times can create more inventory, cash and obsolescence cost than a higher-priced local supplier.
non_examples: Calling a supply chain ethical because suppliers signed a code without checking incentives, audit quality or actual conditions.
applications: trace supply decisions into working capital
real_world_transfer: Identify why a procurement saving can increase total business risk or cash needs.
Question an environmental claim if the business cannot trace key upstream inputs.
assumptions: Supplier data and audit evidence are sufficiently reliable; deeper tiers may be difficult to observe.
limitations: Full traceability can be costly/imperfect; supplier audits can be staged or miss hidden practices; resilience and cost objectives can conflict.

misconceptions.incorrect_belief: The cheapest supplier is the most efficient choice.
misconceptions.correction: Total value includes quality, lead time, inventory, reliability, payment, switching and risk consequences.

interpretation: total-cost comparisons should include consequential costs rather than purchase price alone

nodes.title: Quality, quality control, quality assurance and improvement

teaching_content.core_explanation: Quality is the degree to which an output and its delivery meet relevant requirements and customer expectations. It should not be equated with luxury or high specification. Quality control (QC) focuses on detecting defects or non-conformance, often by inspecting or testing outputs. Quality assurance (QA) focuses on designing and controlling processes so that defects are less likely to occur. Continuous quality improvement goes further by learning from defects, complaints, near misses and process variation. Detecting every bad unit at the end can protect customers but leaves the cost and cause of failure untouched; prevention can reduce scrap, rework and warranty costs but requires process discipline, training and useful measures. In services, quality can include timeliness, accuracy, communication, complaint handling and consistency as well as the core outcome. Customer experience evidence and complaints can therefore act as operational quality data, not merely marketing data.
teaching_content.why_it_matters: Quality affects cost, productivity, customer retention, brand trust and risk across the business.
definitions: quality: fitness for relevant requirements/expectations
quality control: detection of defects/non-conformance in outputs
quality assurance: process systems intended to prevent defects
continuous quality improvement: systematic ongoing learning to reduce causes of failure
important_boundaries: quality is not luxury
QC and QA are complementary but distinct
inspection can catch failure without preventing it
customer complaints measure only reported problems, not all defects
facts: poor quality creates visible and hidden costs
prevention can reduce rework/warranty/returns
quality standards require consistent process execution
mechanisms: process control/training -> fewer defects -> less rework -> productivity/cost benefit
poor quality -> complaints/returns -> brand/cash effects
root-cause improvement -> reduced recurrence
causal_relationships: process quality -> output quality -> customer experience -> retention/reputation
examples: A restaurant can meet food specifications but still deliver poor quality if orders are repeatedly late or inaccurate; service process is part of quality.
non_examples: Saying an expensive product is automatically high quality.
Calling end-of-line inspection a full quality-assurance system.
applications: use complaints/reviews as imperfect quality evidence
real_world_transfer: Explain why rising productivity can be misleading if defect rates also rise.
Identify whether a quality failure is a one-off output defect or a process-system problem.
assumptions: Customer/technical requirements are sufficiently defined and measurable.
limitations: Excessive procedural control can add bureaucracy; not all quality characteristics are easy to measure.

misconceptions.incorrect_belief: Quality assurance means checking the finished product carefully.
misconceptions.correction: That is primarily quality control; assurance focuses on processes intended to prevent defects.

interpretation: rates should distinguish denominator, severity and reporting behaviour
common_errors: treating complaint count as a direct measure of total defects

nodes.title: Location, outsourcing, offshoring and resilience

teaching_content.core_explanation: Location decisions determine where activities are performed and therefore affect labour access/cost, customer proximity, logistics, property, infrastructure, regulation, tax context, supply risk and resilience. Outsourcing means contracting an activity to another organisation; offshoring means relocating activity to another country. They are not synonyms: a company-owned overseas facility is offshored but not outsourced, while a domestic third-party contractor is outsourced but not offshored. Outsourcing can provide specialist capability, flexibility or lower apparent fixed cost, but it creates dependency, contract-management and control challenges. Offshoring can change wage, tax and market access economics while increasing distance, currency, coordination, cultural, legal and geopolitical exposure. Resilience means maintaining or recovering critical activity under disruption; redundancy, multiple suppliers or spare capacity can be rational even though they look less efficient in normal periods. A strong decision compares total cost, capability and risk rather than headline wage or purchase price.
teaching_content.why_it_matters: These decisions combine operations, finance, people, global business and risk, making them strong tests of whole-business reasoning.
definitions: location: geographic placement of business activity
outsourcing: contracting activity to an external provider
offshoring: moving activity to another country
reshoring: returning previously offshored activity closer/home
resilience: ability to absorb, adapt to and recover from disruption
important_boundaries: outsourcing is not offshoring
lower wages are not lower total cost
contracting a task does not transfer every risk
redundancy can be economically valuable
facts: location affects labour, logistics and market access
outsourcing creates supplier dependency
currency and geopolitical changes can alter offshore economics
mechanisms: location -> wage/logistics/infrastructure/regulation -> cost/service
outsourcing -> specialist scale/flexibility -> possible savings but lower direct control
redundancy -> higher normal cost -> lower disruption impact
causal_relationships: offshore sourcing -> longer lead time/currency risk -> inventory/cash/resilience
outsourcing failure -> customer service/reputation even if contractually external
examples: A firm outsources customer support to a domestic specialist: outsourced, not offshored. A firm-owned factory in Vietnam is offshored, not outsourced.
non_examples: Assuming contractual penalties compensate fully for lost customers after supplier failure.
real_world_transfer: Explain why a higher-priced local supplier can be economically preferable after inventory and disruption risk are considered.
assumptions: Relevant costs and risks can be compared over a sensible time horizon.
limitations: Political, exchange-rate and disruption probabilities are uncertain and can change rapidly.

misconceptions.incorrect_belief: Outsourcing transfers the risk to the supplier.
misconceptions.correction: Some contractual responsibility transfers, but the buyer often retains customer, reputation, dependency and continuity exposure.

interpretation: headline labour/purchase cost should be expanded into total landed/system cost where data permit

evidence_of_understanding: evaluate location using total business effects
